list.listitem: Suspect obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) in patients with excessive anxiety, worry about their own thoughts, reassurance seeking, or repetitive behaviors, and use a validated assessment tool to confirm diagnosis. C
Effective treatments include both medications and cognitive-behavioral treatment (CBT) and they can be used together. A
If choosing medication: start with an SSRI at half usual starting dose and titrate upward (depending on response and side effects) to maximal tolerated dose for 4 to 6 weeks before reevaluating. C
If choosing behavioral therapy: refer for CBT that includes exposure to anxiety-arousing obsessions while blocking anxiety-relieving (but OCD-perpetuating) compulsions. A
Recommend appropriate readings for patient education and self-conducted exposure. C

background.definition: OCD is characterized by persistent obsessions (ie, anxiety-arousing, intrusive thoughts), compulsions (ie, repetitive, anxiety-relieving actions or thoughts), or both. The symptoms are not attributable to a medical disorder or drug, are not better explained by another psychiatric diagnosis, and cause significant distress or dysfunction in daily living (DSM-V).

list.listitem: Lifetime prevalence in the general population is usually estimated at around 1.5%, and may occur more in women than men.
Prevalence of OCD symptoms short of criterion-based diagnosis may exceed 8%.
Prevalence in some subgroups (eg, referrals to dermatology clinics) is much higher.
The heterogeneity of OCD and continuing controversy about diagnostic boundaries complicate prevalence estimates.
OCD is rated by the World Health Organization as one of the top 10 most disabling diseases.
The intrusive thoughts and compulsive behaviors are egodystonic and often cause shame and embarassment.
Genetics: There is a four-fold greater lifetime prevalence among primary relatives compared with controls. Twin studies suggest that genetic influences on OCD symptoms range from 45% to 65%.

Other studies have suggested that vulnerability to OCD is greater when the personal or family history is marked by rigid codes of conduct, equating thought and action, perfectionism, and intolerance of ambiguity or uncertainty.

Under stress, a vulnerable individual may experience the onset of intrusive thoughts that are frightening and not easily negated (eg, possible HIV contamination, chance of acting on a reprehensible or dangerous "urge"). Efforts to suppress such thoughts, hypervigilance about thought content, panic in response to such thoughts, and powerfully reinforcing but short-lived relief through neutralizing rituals (eg, repetitive reassurance seeking, replacing "bad" thought with "good" thought) creates a self-reinforcing, self-augmenting vicious cycle.
OCD seems to be underpinned primarily by prefrontal cortex-basal ganglia-thalamic pathways and by the serotonergic and dopaminergic neurotransmitter systems.

Controversy continues about possible immune or inflammatory triggers in the sudden onset or worsening of OCD symptoms in children after group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections, part of a group of disorders called pediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococci (PANDAS).

Patients with excessive anxiety, worry about their own thoughts, reassurance seeking, or repetitive behaviors should be assessed for the presence of anxiety-arousing obsessions or anxiety-relieving compulsions. C
The 18-item, self-administered Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) is appropriate for screening in primary care (). C

list.listitem: See for a brief summary of DSM-V criteria for diagnosis of OCD.

Physicians often confuse OCD and OCPD. OCPD is characterized by pervasive perfectionism, rigidity, orderliness, and/or controlling behaviors that are self-perceived as virtues in contrast to the distressing obsessions of OCD. Despite some overlap in similarly named disorders, most patients with OCD do not have OCPD and most patients with OCPD do not have OCD.

Common presentations include washers, checkers, and compulsive reassurance seekers; however, there is tremendous variability in the content of obsessions and related neutralizing acts from common to very uncommon.

Typical screening questions might include: (1) Unpleasant thoughts you cannot get rid of? (2) Worry that you might somehow "lose control" perhaps even fearing that you might hurt someone? (3) Troubling thoughts or doubts about sexual or religious matters? (4) Repeatedly have to wash/clean, check, count, order, or save things?
Look for signs of doubting, difficulty handling uncertainty, and repetitive thoughts or acts that neutralize distress about obsessive thoughts.

The standard assessment tool for OCD is the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS). However, this well established, clinician-administered instrument can take 20 to 30 minutes to administer. Available online.
For the ages of 6 to 14 years, there is the Children's Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (CY-BOCS), but this is not readily available online.

More practical in primary care is the 18-item, self-administered Obsessive Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) (). Using a cut-off score of 21, OCD was identified relative to nonanxious controls with adequate sensitivity (65.6%) and specificity (63.4%). The OCI-R better assesses compulsions than obsessions such that it should be supplemented with additional screening questions about scrupulosity, sexual, and harming obsessions.

Patients with excessive anxiety, worry about their own thoughts, reassurance seeking, or repetitive behaviors should be evaluated for the presence of anxiety-arousing obsessions or anxiety-relieving compulsions using a validated survey instrument such as the brief, self-administered OCI-R (), the clinician-administered Y-BOCS available online, or the CY-BOCS.
See for a suggested approach to management.
Patient education and self-help strategies, referral for cognitive-behavioral treatment, and medication can be offered as stepped care or in accord with patient preference ().
Medications and cognitive behavioral therapy are both effective.A
SSRIs are the first-line drug treatment. A SSRIs should be titrated to the higher end of the dosing range and evaluated after 4 to 6 weeks at maximal tolerated dose.B
First-line behavioral treatment: CBT that encourages tolerance of uncertainty, exposure to anxiety-arousing obsessions, and delay or blocking of anxiety-relieving compulsions. A
Common alternative medications include a different SSRI, adjunctive CBT, venlafaxine, clomipramine, and augmentation with antipsychotic medication.B
Combination therapy can be superior to monotherapy in some, but is not necessary for all OCD patients. C
First-line drug treatment includes drugs with potent serotonergic effects; SSRIs are usually the first choice because of clomipramine's less favorable side effect profile.
OCD may require eventual dosing at 2 to 4x standard antidepressant doses for longer periods (ie, >1-2 years).

An individual patient data meta-analyis of placebo-controlled trials of SSRIs for OCD found that they are effective, with an odds ratio for treatment response of 2.21 (95% CI 1.72 to 2.83) and a number needed to treat of 7.
Drug comparison trials suggest that venlafaxine may be similarly effective, but RCT-based data are lacking.
SSRIs may also be effective in some cases of overlapping OCD spectrum disorders (eg, hypochondriasis, body dysmorphic disorder).
Augmentation of SSRI therapy with antipsychotics or glutamatergic medications may be helpful in treatment resistant cases.
An algorithm for treatment is shown in .

In patients with very debilitating and refractory OCD, bilateral anterior cingulotomy resulted in 48% mean symptom improvement among about half of patients without significant adverse effects during 24-month follow-up.
Deep brain stimulation resulted in significant symptomatic improvement and functioning among half of patients with very refractory OCD followed for 3 years.
Anterior capsulotomy via stereotactic radiosurgery was found to be effective in 60% to 70% of patients in one systematic review of uncontrolled studies.
Transcranial magnetic stimulation was found to be effective for treatment of OCD in a meta-analysis (SMD -0.51, 95% CI -0.96 to -0.07).
Several meta-analyses suggest that cognitive-behavioral treatment is at least as effective as SSRIs and may be more durable.

Cognitive aspects of treatment address distorted risk assessment, the futility of certainty seeking, and patient education about OCD (eg, compulsions relieve anxiety but perpetuate OCD) as preparation for behavioral exposure.
In children, CBT plus medication is superior to medication alone (NNT = 3).

Exposure and response prevention treatment encourages patients to steer into their anxiety-arousing obsessions while agreeing to delay or refrain from usual neutralizing thoughts or behaviors. This often takes tremendous courage.
A systematic review found that mindfulness-based cognitive therapy is moderately effective.
Once treatment begins, reassurance is usually withheld in favor of working with and tolerating uncertainty.
CBT may also be effective for some cases of OCD spectrum disorders (eg, hypochondriasis, body dysmorphic disorder).
There is inadequate evidence on the use of biofeedback approaches.
In some cases of severe OCD, daily functioning may deteriorate to the point that intensive residential treatment may be necessary.

Rather than referral to the nearest psychiatric inpatient unit, family should be encouraged to investigate specialized residential treatment facilities for OCD (eg, Temple University, Rogers Memorial Hospital, Menninger Clinic).
Significant improvement is evident in 50% to 65% of OCD patients receiving either drug treatment or CBT; however, true remission occurs in only 25% to 38%. B
The effects of CBT that includes exposure and response prevention are more durable than the effects of SSRI treatment after these treatments are discontinued. B
Untreated, OCD may have either a chronic or fluctuating course, but seldom remits entirely.
Drug treatment effects for OCD are most often gradual and partial; 40% to 50% fail to benefit from multiple medication trials.
In a 3-year, prospective follow-up study of SSRIs, 65% of patients had partial remission of OCD, but only 38% had full remission. In the latter group, the probability of subsequent relapse was 60%.
Up to 60% are significantly improved with CBT; however, only about 25% are truly asymptomatic.
The effects of CBT that includes exposure and response prevention appear to be more durable than SSRI treatment after these treatments are discontinued.
Hoarding in the absence of other indications of OCD may be a separate disorder that is often lacking in insight and motivation to change and is often refractory to drug or behavioral treatments.
Patients must understand that seeking "certainty" to remove doubt and repeated neutralization of related distress through compulsions only perpetuates OCD.
It is helpful for patients to understand that OCD is a disorder of doubting and overcontrol rather than of impulsivity and undercontrol.

Recommended readings for patients: (1) OCD: Grayson J. Freedom from OCD: A Personalized Recovery Program for Living with Uncertainty. New York: Tarcher/Putnam, 2003, and (2) Intrusive obsessive thoughts: Baer L. The Imp of the Mind: Exploring the Silent Epidemic of Obsessive Bad Thoughts. New York: Plume, 2002.
Obsessive-Compulsive Foundation: www.ocfoundation.org
True first onset of OCD in old age is uncommon and may reflect CNS impairment.

New onset OCD, often with harming obsessions (ie, "What if I'm not in control and hurt my baby?"), and exacerbation of existing OCD are both common in the postpartum period. If there is no history or current evidence of impulsivity, psychosis, serious depression, or aggressivity, an explanation about obsessions and appropriate readings can be very reassuring to frightened mothers (see Advice for Patients).
Although pediatric OCD has a preteen mean age of onset, onset may occur as early as preschool years.

CBT combined with an SSRI can lead to better outcomes compared to medication alone. For most children, a conservative approach would begin with a CBT trial that includes education and guidance for their parents and teachers.
Tics and ADHD symptoms have been linked to OCD symptoms. Comorbid tic disorders may adversely affect drug treatment, but not CBT.
Sudden OCD onset has been associated with recent streptococcal infection (especially multiple recent infections) and may respond to antibiotic treatment although clinical trials are lacking.
CBT is also effective for this PANDAS subtype of OCD.

cell.label: First-line treatment options: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), SSRI, or both.

cell.label: Is the response adequate after 13 to 20 weekly sessions of CBT?
For medication continue for 1 to 2 years, then consider gradual taper over several months or more. For CBT: provide periodic booster sessions for 3 to 6 months after acute treatment.
Is the response adequate after 8 to 12 total weeks of SSRI (4–6 weeks at maximal tolerable dose) or 13 to 20 weekly sessions of CBT or weekday daily CBT for 3 weeks?

Strategies for Moderate Response: Augment with a second-generation antipsychotic or with CBT (ERP) if not already provided; or add cognitive therapy to ERP.* Strategies for little or no response: Switch to a difference SSRI (may try more than one trial); switch to clomipramine; augment with a second-generation antipsychotic; switch to venlafaxine; switch to mirtazapine.*

Strategies for moderate and for little or no response: switch to a different augmenting second-generation antipsychotic; switch to a different SRI; augment with clomipramine; * augment with buspirone, * pindolol, * morphine sulfate, * inositol, * or a glutamate antagonist ( eg, riluzole, topiramate). * Strategies only for little or no response: switch to D–amphetamine monotherapy; * switch to tramadol monotherapy; * switch to ondansetron monotherapy; * switch to an MAOI. * After first - and second-line strategies have been exhausted, other options that may be considered include transcranial magnetic stimulation, * deep brain stimulation, * and ablative neurosurgery.

feature.caption: Summary of DSM-V Criteria for Diagnosis of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.
feature.feature_body: Presence of obsessions (ie, anxiety-arousing thoughts and images that are experienced as intrusive and inappropriate and cause marked distress; such thoughts, images, or perceived urges are not simply excessive worries about real-life problems; attempts to suppress or neutralize such thoughts; thoughts are recognized as product of patient's own mind) or compulsions (ie, anxiety-relieving, repetitive behaviors or mental acts that aim to neutralize distress or "prevent" bad outcomes; such behaviors or mental acts are not connected in a realistic way with what they are intended to neutralize or they are clearly excessive) or both Presence of either obsessions Presence of obsessions (ie, anxiety-arousing thoughts and images that are experienced as intrusive and inappropriate and cause marked distress; such thoughts, images, or perceived urges are not simply excessive worries about real-life problems; attempts to suppress or neutralize such thoughts; thoughts are recognized as product of patient's own mind) or compulsions (ie, anxiety-relieving, repetitive behaviors or mental acts that aim to neutralize distress or "prevent" bad outcomes; such behaviors or mental acts are not connected in a realistic way with what they are intended to neutralize or they are clearly excessive) or both Presence of either obsessions. Obsessions/compulsions cause marked distress, are time consuming (>1 hour/day), or significantly interfere with functioning. Not better accounted for by another diagnosis. Not secondary to a substance or general medical condition. Data from Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders DSM-V. 5th. Washington, DC: American Psychiatric Association. 2015.
